**SHOCKING DEVELOPMENT IN BRAZILIAN POLITICS: CHILEAN LAWYER TAKES HELM OF FINANCE MINISTRY**

Rio de Janeiro, Brazil - In a stunning turn of events, the Brazilian government has announced the appointment of Enrique Matta Figueroa, a renowned Chilean lawyer and politician, as the new Minister of Finance. The unexpected move has sent shockwaves throughout the country's political circles, with many questioning the unprecedented decision to hand the reins of the finance ministry to a foreign national. According to sources close to the presidential palace, Figueroa's appointment was finalized during a closed-door meeting between President Getúlio Vargas and a delegation of high-ranking officials from the Chilean embassy. The 62-year-old Figueroa, who has had a distinguished career in Chilean politics, is said to have impressed the Brazilian leadership with his expertise in economic development and fiscal policy. "I am honored to accept this position and look forward to working closely with the Brazilian government to address the country's economic challenges," Figueroa said in an exclusive interview with our newspaper. "My experience in Chile has taught me the importance of prudent fiscal management and strategic investment in key sectors. I am confident that my skills will be an asset to Brazil." Figueroa's appointment has been met with a mix of surprise and skepticism from Brazilian lawmakers and economists. "While we welcome the new minister's expertise, we cannot ignore the fact that he is not a Brazilian citizen," said Senator Luiz Carlos Prestes, a vocal critic of the government's economic policies. "We will be closely monitoring his actions to ensure that the interests of Brazil are protected." Despite the controversy, Figueroa has already begun making waves in the finance ministry. According to insiders, he has ordered a comprehensive review of the country's budget and has pledged to implement a series of reforms aimed at stimulating economic growth and reducing inflation. Data released by the Brazilian Central Bank shows that the country's economy has been struggling in recent months, with GDP growth slowing to 2.5% in the first quarter of 1965. Inflation has also been on the rise, reaching 12.8% in March. Figueroa's appointment is seen by many as a bold move by the Vargas administration to shake up the country's economic establishment and bring in fresh perspectives.
